subject: Critical Thinking
title: Survivorship Bias: The Silent Evidence Problem
description: A short lesson to help you apply Survivorship Bias: The Silent Evidence Problem.

hook.text: WWII planes returned covered in bullet holes. Engineers planned to armor those spots.

buildup.text: The planes that got hit in other places didn't come back. You only saw survivors — not the full picture.

discovery.text: Survivorship bias: we draw conclusions from visible successes and ignore invisible failures.

twist.text: 'Bill Gates dropped out & became a billionaire.' True. Also: millions of dropouts aren't billionaires.

climax.text: Self-help books, startup advice, and success stories all suffer from survivorship bias. The dead don't write memoirs.

punchline.text: Before you copy the winners, count the losers you can't see.

quiz.question: Why did Abraham Wald suggest armoring undamaged areas of planes?
options: Planes hit in those areas didn't survive to be studied

details.summary: Survivorship bias focuses on successes while ignoring failures that are no longer visible. Studying only college dropouts who became billionaires ignores millions who dropped out and struggled.
details.whyItMatters: Survivorship bias distorts advice, strategy, and risk assessment because the failures that could teach us the most have disappeared from view.
takeaways: Visible successes are not representative of all attempts
WWII bullet hole analysis is the classic survivorship bias example
Always ask: where are the failures I cannot see?

faq.question: What is the WWII airplane story that illustrates survivorship bias?
faq.answer: Engineers wanted to armor the parts of returning planes that had the most bullet holes. Abraham Wald pointed out they should armor the parts without holes, because planes hit there never made it back. The survivors misled the analysis.

faq.question: How does survivorship bias affect career and business advice?
faq.answer: We study successful entrepreneurs and extract their common traits, ignoring that failed entrepreneurs had the same traits. The advice becomes 'do what survivors did' when the real lesson requires studying failures too.
